title: Problem Introduction
content: Erdős Problem #729 asks whether the divisibility bound $a + b \leq n + O(\log n)$ for $a!b! \mid n!$ persists when ignoring small primes. Barreto and Leeham proved it does, adapting the technique from Problem #728. The problem connects the local (prime-by-prime) structure of factorial divisibility to a global arithmetic constraint.
mathContext: If $a!b! \mid n!$, Erdős proved $a + b \leq n + O(\log n)$ in 1968. Problem 729 asks: can this be beaten if we allow the denominator of $n!/(a!b!)$ to have small prime factors $p \leq C$?

title: Factorial p-adic Valuation
content: Defines `factorialPadicVal p n` as $\sum_{i \geq 1} \lfloor n/p^i \rfloor$, computing $v_p(n!)$ via Legendre's formula. The axiom `legendre_formula` equates this with Mathlib's `padicValNat p n.factorial`. The sum is finite since $\lfloor n/p^i \rfloor = 0$ for $p^i > n$, so only $O(\log_p n)$ terms are nonzero.
mathContext: $v_p(n!) = \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \lfloor n/p^i \rfloor = \frac{n - s_p(n)}{p-1}$, where $s_p(n)$ is the digit sum in base $p$

title: Legendre's Formula Axiom
content: Axiomatizes the equality between Mathlib's `padicValNat p n.factorial` and the explicit summation `factorialPadicVal p n`. This bridges the abstract p-adic valuation in Mathlib with the concrete computational formula. A proof would require showing that $\sum \lfloor n/p^i \rfloor$ counts the exact multiplicity of $p$ in $n!$.

title: Factorial Divisibility
content: Defines `DividesFactorial n a b` as $a! \cdot b! \mid n!$. When $a + b = n$, this is equivalent to $\binom{n}{a}$ being an integer (always true). When $a + b > n$, the quotient $n!/(a!b!)$ may not be integral. The condition is equivalent to $v_p(a!) + v_p(b!) \leq v_p(n!)$ for all primes $p$, connecting divisibility to Legendre's formula.
mathContext: $\text{DividesFactorial}(n, a, b) \iff a! \cdot b! \mid n! \iff \forall p \text{ prime},\, v_p(a!) + v_p(b!) \leq v_p(n!)$

title: Erdős 1968 Classical Result
content: Axiomatizes Erdős's 1968 result: if $a!b! \mid n!$ then $a + b \leq n + O(\log n)$. The proof uses only the constraint from $p = 2$: since $v_2(n!) = n - s_2(n)$ and $s_2(n) \leq \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1$, the inequality $v_2(a!) + v_2(b!) \leq v_2(n!)$ gives $a + b - s_2(a) - s_2(b) \leq n - s_2(n)$, hence $a + b \leq n + s_2(a) + s_2(b) - s_2(n) \leq n + O(\log n)$.
mathContext: $a!b! \mid n! \implies a + b \leq n + O(\log n)$, proved using $v_2(n!) = n - s_2(n)$ where $s_2(n) = O(\log n)$

title: Powers of Two Argument
content: The theorem `erdos_proof_via_powers_of_two` forwards to `erdos_1968_classical`, documenting the proof strategy. The elegance of Erdős's argument is that a single prime ($p = 2$) suffices: $v_2(n!) = n - s_2(n)$ gives $a + b = (a - s_2(a)) + (b - s_2(b)) + s_2(a) + s_2(b) \leq (n - s_2(n)) + s_2(a) + s_2(b) \leq n + O(\log n)$. This is the key insight that Problem 729 tests: if one prime controls the bound, can ignoring a few primes weaken it?
mathContext: $v_2(a!) + v_2(b!) \leq v_2(n!) \implies (a - s_2(a)) + (b - s_2(b)) \leq n - s_2(n) \implies a + b \leq n + s_2(a) + s_2(b) - s_2(n)$

title: Small Primes
content: Defines `SmallPrimes C` as the set of primes $p$ with $p \leq C$. This is a finite set (by the finiteness of primes below a bound). The problem asks what happens when we allow the denominator of $n!/(a!b!)$ to contain factors from these primes. The set depends on the real parameter $C$, which serves as the threshold separating 'small' from 'large' primes.
mathContext: $\text{SmallPrimes}(C) = \{p \in \mathbb{P} : p \leq C\}$, a finite set of cardinality $\pi(C)$

title: Relaxed Divisibility
content: Defines `DividesFactorialModSmall n a b C`: there exists a $C$-smooth number $k$ (all prime factors $\leq C$) such that $k \cdot a! \cdot b! \mid n!$. Multiplying by $k$ 'absorbs' the small prime factors in the denominator. Equivalently, $v_p(a!) + v_p(b!) \leq v_p(n!)$ need only hold for primes $p > C$, since any deficit at small primes can be compensated by $k$.
mathContext: $\text{DividesFactorialModSmall}(n,a,b,C) \iff \exists k \in \mathbb{N},\, (\forall p \mid k,\, p \leq C) \land k \cdot a! \cdot b! \mid n!$

title: The Question
content: Defines `InfinitelyManyExceptions C` as a $\forall N, \exists$ statement: for every bound $N$, there exist $a, b, n$ with $n > N$, $a + b > n + C \log n$, and the relaxed divisibility holds. This is the formal negation of 'the bound $a + b \leq n + C \log n$ holds for all sufficiently large $n$'. The use of $\forall N, \exists$ captures 'infinitely many' without invoking cardinality.
mathContext: $\text{InfinitelyManyExceptions}(C) \equiv \forall N,\, \exists a,b,n:\, n > N \land a+b > n + C\log n \land \text{DividesFactorialModSmall}(n,a,b,C)$

title: Barreto-Leeham Theorem
content: Axiomatizes the main result: $\neg\text{InfinitelyManyExceptions}(C)$ for all $C > 0$. The answer to Erdős's question is NO. The proof adapts the technique from Problem #728: for any prime $p > C$, the $p$-adic constraint $v_p(a!) + v_p(b!) \leq v_p(n!)$ is unaffected by the $C$-smooth correction factor $k$, so the Erdős-style bound follows from any single large prime.
mathContext: $\forall C > 0,\, \neg\text{InfinitelyManyExceptions}(C)$: the logarithmic bound cannot be defeated by ignoring finitely many primes

title: Extended Bound
content: Axiomatizes an explicit quantitative version: there exists $D > 0$ such that the relaxed divisibility $\text{DividesFactorialModSmall}(n,a,b,C)$ implies $a + b \leq n + D \log n$. This is stronger than negating infinitely many exceptions because it provides a uniform bound for ALL triples, not just eventually. The constant $D$ may depend on $C$.
mathContext: $\forall C > 0,\, \exists D > 0,\, \forall n,a,b:\, \text{DividesFactorialModSmall}(n,a,b,C) \implies a+b \leq n + D\log n$

title: Proof Strategy via Large Primes
content: Axiomatizes the key step: for primes $p > C$, the $p$-adic constraint $v_p(a!) + v_p(b!) \leq v_p(n!)$ holds even under the relaxed condition, because the correction factor $k$ is $C$-smooth and hence $v_p(k) = 0$. This means the constraint from each large prime individually forces $a + b \leq n + O(\log n)$, and no finite set of 'ignored' primes can weaken the bound.
mathContext: $p > C \implies v_p(k) = 0 \implies v_p(a!) + v_p(b!) \leq v_p(n!)$, so each large prime independently enforces the Erdős bound

title: Digit Sum
content: Defines `digitSum p n` recursively: $s_p(0) = 0$ and $s_p(n) = (n \bmod p) + s_p(\lfloor n/p \rfloor)$ for $n > 0$. This computes the sum of digits of $n$ in base $p$. The function appears in Legendre's identity $v_p(n!) = (n - s_p(n))/(p-1)$. For $p = 2$, the identity simplifies to $v_2(n!) = n - s_2(n)$, the heart of Erdős's original proof.

title: Legendre's Identity
content: Axiomatizes the identity $v_p(n!) = (n - s_p(n))/(p-1)$ for primes $p \geq 2$. This is equivalent to the summation formula $\sum \lfloor n/p^i \rfloor = (n - s_p(n))/(p-1)$, a standard identity in combinatorial number theory. The proof proceeds by writing $n$ in base $p$ and collecting terms. The hypothesis $p \geq 2$ is redundant (all primes satisfy this) but makes the division by $p-1$ well-defined.
mathContext: $v_p(n!) = \frac{n - s_p(n)}{p-1}$, where $s_p(n) = \sum_{j} d_j$ for $n = \sum_j d_j p^j$ in base $p$

title: Legendre for p = 2 (proved)
content: Proves $v_2(n!) = n - s_2(n)$ outright from Mathlib's Legendre theorem `sub_one_mul_padicValNat_factorial`, which states $(p-1)\,v_p(n!) = n - (\text{digits}_p\,n).\text{sum}$. For $p = 2$ the factor $p - 1 = 1$ collapses, giving the identity directly. The helper `digitSum_eq_digits_sum` bridges the file's recursive `digitSum 2 n` to Mathlib's `(Nat.digits 2 n).sum`. This replaced the former `legendre_identity` axiom, which has been deleted — the OQ-02 question (can `legendre_for_two` be completed via Mathlib's padicValNat machinery?) is answered yes.
mathContext: $v_2(n!) = n - s_2(n)$, the simplest case of Legendre's identity since $p - 1 = 1$

title: Factorial Rigidity
content: Axiomatizes the conceptual insight: the constraint $a + b \leq n + O(\log n)$ arises from all primes collectively, and no finite set of exceptions can weaken it. This is `factorial_rigidity`, essentially restating `barreto_leeham_bound` in different terms to emphasize the rigidity interpretation. The result reveals that factorial divisibility is a global phenomenon controlled by the entire prime structure.
mathContext: The $p$-adic constraints $\{v_p(a!) + v_p(b!) \leq v_p(n!)\}_{p > C}$ collectively force $a + b \leq n + O(\log n)$, independent of $C$

title: Binomial Rigidity (sorry)
content: States that when $a + b = n$, the quotient $n!/(a!b!) = \binom{n}{a}$ is always an integer, i.e., `DividesFactorial n a b` holds. This is the second `sorry` in the file. A proof would use the well-known fact that binomial coefficients are integers, available in Mathlib as `Nat.choose_spec` or via the multinomial coefficient theory.

title: Main Problem Statement
content: Proves `erdos_729_statement` by combining `erdos_1968_classical` (the 1968 bound) and `barreto_leeham_theorem` (the extension). The proof is a simple `constructor` splitting the conjunction, with each half forwarded to its respective axiom. This packages both results into a single statement that Erdős's bound is both true and robust.
mathContext: $(\forall n,a,b,\, a!b! \mid n! \implies a+b \leq n + O(\log n)) \;\land\; (\forall C > 0,\, \neg\text{InfinitelyManyExceptions}(C))$

title: Summary Theorem
content: Proves `erdos_729_summary` combining the negative answer ($\neg\text{InfinitelyManyExceptions}(C)$) with the explicit quantitative bound ($a + b \leq n + D \log n$ under the relaxed condition). The proof again splits with `constructor` and forwards to the two Barreto-Leeham axioms. This provides the complete answer: NO, and here is the explicit bound.
mathContext: $(\forall C > 0,\, \neg\text{InfinitelyManyExceptions}(C)) \;\land\; (\forall C > 0,\, \exists D > 0,\, \text{uniform bound } a+b \leq n + D\log n)$
